title: What Materials Do Plants Need to Grow?

opener.title: What Materials Do Plants Need to Grow?
opener.question: A tiny seed grows into a giant tree. Where does all of that wood come from?
opener.alt: An opening film that zooms from Earth to Belgium, to a willow tree, to a leaf, to a tiny opening in the leaf, to leaf cells, and finally to a drawing of gas molecules in the air.

k-warmup.text: Every page in the Notebook Chain was written by a scientist who tested an idea. Today's page is about a willow tree. Before you read it, make a prediction. The tree slice has ten pieces. Tap Soil, Water, Air, or Sunlight to fill each piece. Then write one reason. Your prediction is saved until Part 4.

k-words.text: These six words will help you read today's page. Tap a word sticker. I'll read it to you, and the card shows what it means. Try to tap all six.

k-part1.text: This is the real page from 1648, written in Latin. Tap a yellow line, and I'll read it to you in plain English. Then hunt for two lines: the one where he says what he did not weigh, and the one where he says what the tree was made of.

k-part2.text: Can air have mass? Let's test it. The ball is sitting on a kitchen scale. Press Pump to push air into the ball, and watch the number on the scale. Then decide what that tells you about the air around a leaf.

k-part3.text: Some stores call this bag plant food. Tap the three numbers on the label to find out what they mean. Then compare the nutrients in the whole bag with the weight the willow gained.

k-part4.text: Now run van Helmont's five years. Drag the year slider and watch both scales. He only weighed things at the start and at the end, so read those numbers carefully. Fill in the Change boxes. Then compare your tree with the evidence.

k-wow.text: Van Helmont measured carefully, and his numbers were right. But his idea, water alone, left out something that was around the tree the whole time. Good scientists can be careful and still miss something. That's why the chain keeps going.

k-assign.text: Now it's your turn to add a page to the chain. Answer the two Part B questions. In Part C, write what van Helmont did well and what he missed. Then use the planner to build your C-E-R.

predict.title: Slice the tree: make a prediction
predict.intro: A scientist's willow tree gained 164 pounds in 5 years. You'll meet him in Part 1. Where did those pounds come from? This real slice of a tree trunk is cut into 10 pieces. Each piece stands for about 16 pounds of new tree.
job: Tap Soil, Water, Air, or Sunlight to fill the next piece of the slice.
Use more pieces for the place you think more of the weight came from.
Write one reason in the box below.
predict.saved: 🌳 Your prediction is saved. You'll compare it with the evidence in Part 4 of The Lesson.
predict.reasonPrompt: Why did you build your tree this way? Write at least one full sentence.
predict.sliceCredit: Photo: a real tree-trunk slice. Kelsey Todd, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to hear it and see what it means.

words.def: A living thing. Plants, animals, and even tiny bacteria are organisms.
A gas in the air (called CO₂). Plants pull it in through tiny holes in their leaves.
H₂O. Plants take it in through their roots from the soil.
The plant structures that catch sunlight and pull in air for making food.
The plant structures underground. They pull water and nutrients out of the soil.
A living thing that makes its own food. Plants are producers. They don't eat other things.

source.kicker: Part 1 game · A real page from 1648
source.title: Van Helmont's own words
source.intro: This is the real page where Jan Baptist van Helmont wrote up his willow experiment. It is in Latin, the language scientists used then. It was printed in 1648, after he died.
job: Tap each yellow line to hear it read in plain English.
Then do the two hunts next to the page.

lines.en: I took a clay pot. I put in 200 pounds of soil that I had dried in an oven, and I wet it with rainwater.
In it I planted a willow stem that weighed 5 pounds.
After exactly five years, the tree that grew weighed 169 pounds and about 3 ounces.
Whenever it needed water, I gave it only rainwater or distilled (very clean) water.
The pot was big and set into the ground. To keep blowing dust out of the soil, I covered the top with a tin-coated iron plate full of small holes.
I did not count the weight of the leaves that fell off in the four autumns.
At the end, I dried the soil again. It weighed the same 200 pounds, less about 2 ounces.
So 164 pounds of wood, bark, and roots had come from water alone.

asks.q: Hunt 1. Find the line where van Helmont says he did NOT weigh something.
asks.yes: Yes. He never weighed the leaves that fell each autumn. The tree made those leaves too, so it really built even MORE than 164 pounds. Good scientists write down what they did not measure.
asks.no: Not that one. Look for the line about something that fell off the tree.

asks.q: Hunt 2. Find the line where he says what the tree was made of.
asks.yes: Yes. He decided the tree came from water alone. Hold on to that idea. You'll check it in Part 4.
asks.no: Not that one. Look near the end, where he uses the number 164.

source.credit: Jan Baptist van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae (Amsterdam: Elzevier, 1648), page 109. Wellcome Collection, via Internet Archive. Public domain. English: a plain-language translation written for this lesson.

air.title: Can air have mass?
air.why: Many people think air weighs nothing, because you can't see it or feel it sitting on you. Let's test that idea with a ball and a kitchen scale.
job: Press Pump to push air into the ball.
Watch the number on the scale after each pump.
Then answer the question below the scale.
air.note: A model based on a real soccer ball: pumping it up adds about 6 grams of air.
air.q: What does the scale tell you?

options.t: Air has mass. Adding air made the ball heavier.
The pump pushed down on the scale.
options.hint: Look again: the pump never touches the scale. Only the ball sits on it.
Read the scale again. Compare the number before you pumped with the number now.

air.win: Right. Air is matter, so it has mass. Carbon dioxide is part of the air, so it has mass too. A leaf pulls in carbon dioxide through its stomata every sunny day, for years. Tiny bits add up.

bag.title: Is fertilizer really plant food?
bag.why: Some bags of fertilizer say “plant food.” Fertilizer adds nutrients, minerals like nitrogen. Let's read a label like a scientist and see how much of a bag is nutrients.
job: Tap each of the three numbers on the label.
Work out how many pounds of nutrients are in the whole bag.
Then decide what fertilizer is really like.

nums.name: nitrogen (N)
nums.tip: 10 out of every 100 parts is nitrogen.

nums.name: phosphate (P)
nums.tip: 10 out of every 100 parts is phosphate.

nums.name: potash (K)
nums.tip: 10 out of every 100 parts is potash.

bag.exampleNote: Example label made for this lesson. Real bags list three numbers like this.
bag.ask: Add them up: 30 out of every 100 parts are the three main nutrients. How many pounds of nutrients are in this 20-pound bag?
bag.answerHint: 30 out of 100 is 3 out of 10. What is 3 tenths of 20 pounds?
bag.compare: A whole bag has about 6 pounds of nutrients. Van Helmont's willow gained 164 pounds, and he added zero fertilizer.

stamps.t: Vitamins: a small help to stay healthy
The main meal: what the plant is built from
stamps.hint: Could 6 pounds of nutrients build 164 pounds of tree? And van Helmont used none.

bag.win: Yes. Nutrients are like vitamins for you: a tiny amount keeps a plant healthy. They are not where the plant's weight comes from.

timelapse.kicker: Part 4 game · Run the five years
timelapse.title: Part 4 · The Willow Tree Data
timelapse.intro: In a book published in 1648, Jan van Helmont described one of the first careful plant experiments. Now run his five years yourself and read his scales.
job: Drag the year slider from 0 to 5.
Read both scales at Year 0 and at Year 5.
Fill in the two Change boxes.
Then compare your tree with the evidence.
timelapse.note: Van Helmont only weighed at the start and at the end. In between, the scales show “not weighed,” because he didn't measure those years.

inputs.label: Soil change
inputs.hint: 200 lb minus 199 lb 14 oz. There are 16 ounces in a pound.

realNotes.soil: About 2 ounces. That's a pinch, not even one piece.
realNotes.water: About half. Much of a living tree is water, and water helps build the sugar.
realNotes.air: About half. The carbon in wood comes from carbon dioxide in the air. Dry wood is about half carbon.
realNotes.sun: Zero pounds. Sunlight is energy, not matter. It powers the building but adds no weight.

wow.quote: So 164 pounds of wood, bark, and roots had come from
wow.add: water AND carbon dioxide from the air
wow.line: His numbers were careful and correct. His idea missed the air.

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: The willow gained about 164 pounds in 5 years.
The soil lost only about 2 ounces.
Pumping air into a ball made it heavier, so air has mass.
Leaves take in carbon dioxide through tiny openings called stomata.
A 20-pound bag of fertilizer has only about 6 pounds of nutrients.
Sunlight is energy, not matter, so it adds no weight.

Part B: questions 1 and 2, in complete sentences.
Part C: your notebook page (what van Helmont did well, and what he missed).
C-E-R: a claim, at least two pieces of evidence, and your reasoning.

data.title: Watch Earth breathe
data.intro: Scientists on Mauna Loa, a mountain in Hawaii, have measured the carbon dioxide in the air every month since 1958. Here are the last ten years.
job: Drag across the graph to read the months.
Find the month when carbon dioxide is lowest each year.
data.ask: In which months does the line dip each year?

opts.t: Summer into fall (about May to October)

opts.hint: Look at where each zigzag hits its bottom. Drag to a low point and read the month.

data.win: Yes. Every spring and summer, the plants of the Northern Hemisphere grow leaves and pull carbon dioxide out of the air, the same way van Helmont's willow did. You are watching the whole planet's plants breathe in. (The line also climbs year after year, mostly because people burn fuels like gasoline and coal.)
data.credit: Data: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa Observatory monthly mean CO₂ (public data), Jan 2016 to Sep 2026.

cabinet.title: A 300-million-year-old tree
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of a fossil Calamites stem, a ribbed, segmented piece of stone shaped like a thick stalk.
cabinet.text: This is a real fossil from the Smithsonian: part of the stem of a Calamites, a giant plant related to today's horsetails. It grew in a swampy forest in what is now Kentucky about 300 million years ago. Like van Helmont's willow, it built its body from carbon dioxide and water. Forests of plants like this, buried for millions of years, slowly turned into coal.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Calamites sp., USNM P33652, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Department of Paleobiology. CC0.

footage.title: A year of Earth's carbon dioxide, from NASA
footage.intro: NASA scientists used a supercomputer model to show how carbon dioxide moves around Earth during one year (2006). This clip speeds the whole year into 20 seconds. Red and orange mean more carbon dioxide. Blue means less.
look: Watch the top half of the world. It turns red in winter and spring.
Then watch it fade toward blue in summer, when plants and trees are full of leaves.
Ask yourself: where is all that carbon dioxide going?
footage.credit: Video: “A Year in the Life of Earth's CO₂,” NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio, GEOS-5 model (public domain). Sped up for this lesson.
